import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 218

*Reference:* [erdosproblems.com/218](https://www.erdosproblems.com/218)
-/

namespace Erdos218

/--
The set of indices $n$ for which a prime gap is followed by a larger or equal prime gap has a
natural density of $\frac 1 2$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_218.variants.le : {n | primeGap n ≤ primeGap (n + 1)}.HasDensity <| 1 / 2 := by
  sorry

/--
The set of indices $n$ for which a prime gap is preceded by a larger or equal prime gap has a
natural density of $\frac 1 2$.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_218.variants.ge : {n | primeGap (n + 1) ≤ primeGap n}.HasDensity <| 1 / 2 := by
  sorry

/--
There are infinitely many indices $n$ such that the prime gap at $n$ is equal to the prime gap
at $n+1$. This is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many arithmetic progressions of
length $3$, see `erdos_141.variants.infinite_three`.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem erdos_218.variants.infinite_equal_prime_gap : {n | primeGap n = primeGap (n + 1)}.Infinite := by
  sorry

end Erdos218

findings.description: The explanatory sentence at lines 45–46 says this is equivalent to infinitely many “arithmetic progressions of length 3,” omitting “of consecutive primes.” Equal adjacent prime gaps characterize three consecutive primes in arithmetic progression, not arbitrary three-term progressions or even arbitrary three-term prime progressions. Infinitely many unrestricted prime progressions are already known. The Lean proposition itself correctly states the equal-gap conjecture.
findings.source_evidence: Erdős, Some problems on the distribution of prime numbers (1955), PDF p. 3, explicitly asks whether d_{n+1}=d_n has infinitely many solutions (https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1955-12.pdf). The section “Consecutive primes in arithmetic progression” at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primes_in_arithmetic_progression distinguishes these from unrestricted prime progressions, whose infinitude follows from Green–Tao. The referenced local declaration Erdos141.erdos_141.variants.infinite_three likewise concerns consecutive primes.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the sentence to: “This is equivalent to the existence of infinitely many arithmetic progressions of length 3 consisting of consecutive primes, see `erdos_141.variants.infinite_three`.”

reformulations.difference: Compared with Erdős’s original 1955 strict-increase formulation d_{n+1}>d_n, Lean uses the weak inequality primeGap n ≤ primeGap (n+1).
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The weak-increase set is the disjoint union of the strict-increase set and E={n | primeGap n=primeGap (n+1)}. Erdős–Rényi’s estimate in their 1950 Theorem 2 implies that E has natural density zero. Consequently the two increase sets have the same density whenever either density exists. The scratch file proves the density-transfer equivalence conditional on E having density zero; it does not formalize the Erdős–Rényi estimate. Zero-based prime indexing merely translates the indices by one and does not change density.

reformulations.difference: Relative to the original strict-increase conjecture, this declaration instead states density 1/2 for weak decreases.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: The weak-decrease set {n | primeGap (n+1) ≤ primeGap n} is exactly the complement of the strict-increase set {n | primeGap n < primeGap (n+1)}. A set has natural density 1/2 iff its complement does. This equivalence, including the complement-density lemma for the repository’s HasDensity definition, was proved in /workspace/review/equivalence.lean without using the conjecture declarations.

sources_consulted: P. Erdős, Some problems on the distribution of prime numbers (1955), especially PDF p. 3: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1955-12.pdf
P. Erdős and A. Rényi, Some problems and results on consecutive primes, Simon Stevin 27 (1950), 115–125, especially Theorem 2: https://www.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1950-12.pdf
review.notes: No misformalization was found in the three theorem propositions. The cited erdosproblems.com page remained Cloudflare-blocked despite descriptive User-Agent headers; verification instead used the original literature, a transcription, linked OEIS entries, and the current Erdős problem database. The retrieved database records 218 and 141 as open, and Wikipedia still records balanced-prime infinitude as open. Lean checks in /workspace/review/scratch.lean and /workspace/review/equivalence.lean compile without errors. They verify the real-valued natural-density definition, finite counting intervals, harmless N=0 denominator convention, positivity and non-default values of prime gaps, small comparison cases, and the identity relating equal gaps to three consecutive primes in arithmetic progression. The reviewed file was not modified.
